'''2003 World Championship Day 2 Jonny Chu DS This Deal Is Getting Worse All The Time''' was the Dark Side constructed list played by [[Jonny Chu]] at [[2003 World Championship]] (Day 2); the list below is as posted on DeckTech by Jonathan "jonnychu" Chu (2003-09-03).<ref name="src">[http://www.decktech.net/starwarsccg/decks/decks.php?deck=30220 Speed Deal w/ Ket Maliss]. Preserved copy: [https://web.archive.org/web/20060514235247/http://www.decktech.net:80/starwarsccg/decks/decks.php?deck=30220 Internet Archive]</ref>

== Original post ==

'''Speed Deal w/ Ket Maliss'''
* '''Author:''' Jonathan "jonnychu" Chu
* '''Published:''' September 3, 2003
* '''Rating:''' 4.96
* '''Description:''' This deck sets up in space with matching pilots and on the ground with deal in two turns.

=== Strategy ===

This Deal deck went 4-0 for me in Day 2 of DragonCon 2003, including wins over Brian Hunter, Matt Lush and Justin Desai.

History:

I was in Aspen, CO for the summer and was OOC for a little over eleven weeks, from just before Virtual Set 5 was released up until a week before DragonCon. That being said, my access to information and especially playtesting was awfully limited. Still, I heard interesting things about decks played at different tournaments throughout the summer, including the dominance of Walkers at Origins and random state championships.

Last year my Speed Watto went 4-0 at Worlds, posting wins of over 30 against three top players and a nail-biting win of 7 over its worst matchup, Throne Room mains. The basic premise of the deck was simple: come down fast and hard and satisfy both Honor and Battle Plan at the same time. Thus was Watto combined with Ket Maliss, which guarantees cheap, decent guys with the likes of Baron and ship, perhaps the most economical way to hold space early.

This year, with Watto made unplayable by Tauntaun Bones, a new platform was needed. I felt like since many of the successful decks out there at the time were slow (Walkers) or relied on a powerful setup engine like Senate (which has built-in ground immunity due to the power=0 text of the site), a quick-strike deck would wreak havoc in a meta consisting of slow decks beating on equally slow decks.

Thus was Speed Deal born. The Dark Deal engine appealed instantaneously for multiple reasons: (1), free Secret Plans/IAO; (2), free way of pulling a system (no Mob Pts needed); (3), immunity to creature attacks; (4), immunity to Projection of a Skywalker and ways to combat other popular ways of force drain denial (challenge Menace Fades in space); and (5), take advantage of wasted card slots most Light decks pack now for anti-Senate and anti-Walker hate.

Play:

The deck is straightforward but surprisingly difficult to play. I say this not meaning to brag about anything, but simply as truth: the deck is amazingly flexible and each game presents a different set of solutions and order of solutions to whatever your opponent throws at you. I played against myself in Colorado well over 30 games of Speed Deal vs Throne Room mains, the matchup I thought would be most difficult, and every single game was different depending on the draws of both decks. I also know the difficulty of playing this deck through experience; in testing before Day 2, Mike Gemme, Justin Desai and Clint Hays all beat me down game after game with different decks. I ended up adding several of the cards (Stop Motion and Blast Door Controls) because of the severe beatings they gave me, but also playing against each different decktype showed me even more what to do/not to do in many ways. More on that in deck-to-deck matchups at the bottom.

In most matchups, the start is similar. You draw your hand. You pull your four guys with Ket Maliss during consequent turns, so by your turn 2 you have at least everyone but Dannik in your hand. Since you play five matching ships/pilots and two Short Range Fighters combos to boot, the odds of you getting one of those twelve cards is fairly high. Pull your sites using I'm Sorry, activate, and dive into your deck using your objective. You are checking for several things now:

(1) Number of pilots/ships and the pullers

(2) Bespin and Bespin Cloud City

(3) Number of Accelerates and Dark Deals

(4) Ghhhks/Masterful Moves

To set up Deal on turn 2, you will probably just draw, but if you want to play it safe (usually against a ground-based deck) you may want to deploy a matching pilot combo (whichever, they all deploy so cheap) now to the system to put some pressure on early. If you activated either a Bespin, Cloud City, Deal or Accelerate, or have one in your hand, for a certainty you can deploy Deal turn 2, because on turn 2 you should be activating at least eight off yourself, and that's usually enough to deploy your three guys for deal (Hem, Greedo and Reegesk for four) and a ship (Zuckuss/MH or Black 2/DS-61-2 for 3, or Dengar or OS-72-10 for 2) to the sector, plus move him to the system to satisfy Battle Plan.

Once the Deal is set up, likely your opponent will drop down Obi-Wan or someone to hammer you. This is totally cool. For sure you can set up the Deal with confidence if you have a Ghhhk or a Masterful Move and enough force (remember to save for Draw Their Fire), but some of the time you don't even need it because Reegesk is base power 5, 6 if you have one ship at Cloud City. So he comes down and wipes the floor with Reegesk? Next turn you come down with the 11 power Maul and deliver Obi-Wan a beating, and if you have the force you can even follow with a Dannik Jerriko soup-eating monster to make sure he never comes back. Hell, if Dannik stays around he's going to be a power 11 base too!

Specific card choices:

Stop Motion (v) and Blast Door Controls: These weren't in the deck originally but it needs them desperately. If the light side player can Barrier or Dodge away you can never apply the re-beats on his guy who beat down your dude. That little (or big) overflow is key.

Ability, Ability, Ability over Search and Destroy: originally the deck had both, but S&D always got cancelled when EPP Luke came down and wasted Reegesk. Ability^3 is key against ground decks like Senate and Throne Room.

Hem Dazon (v) over Beedo or anyone good: he's actually decent. Hem Dazon in space is key to cracking Home One's immunity. He is great as a crappy Reactor Terminal. For two force you get a four forfeit guy you're guaranteed to have for Deal.

Dark Maneuvers/Tallon Roll: I used to play 2 and trimmed it down, but you gotta have it in here. Worst case scenario you can use it as a Ghhhk, or best case you can Tallon Roll away an empty ship with Legendary on it oclobersky X-wing with cannons.

Bad Feeling: big. Fetch this as soon as you can, preferably before or on the turn you flip. EPP OBi, Luke and jacked-up Lando each cost 8 to deploy to CC. The merits of BFHI are well-documented.

Obsidian 10 and matching guy: this guy is a choice call. He helps a lot vs Watch Your Step adding an extra destiny, and he's a 7 base for Tallon Roll for two force. I could see using another Zuckuss/MH instead, though.

Prophetess (v): she is a monster, much better than the 6 or 8 deploy Darth Sidious who pretty much blows in a fast deck.

Lower Corridor: the extra power +2 here usually translates to two more cards off the top for him.

Also you could start this card as your site vs Throne Room, stack space and play Ability^3.

Docking Bay: necessary to play Deal if your opponent comes down to your starting site first turn.

Oota-Goota Solo?: use it with Dengar or Zuckuss on the ground if you really need to kill that random guy.

No Emperor? --- crappy in an essentially hit-and-kill deck.

No Janus? --- same, six force for a power 2 guy with useless game text (games shouldn't last long) is bad.

No big beefy ability 4 guys in general? --- the speed is the shocker in the deck. Most Deal decks play Deal by turn 4 or 5. This trims it down to 2 at the cost of efficient guys who actually do something. The low cost Goo Nee Tay immunity is more important.

No Stunning Leader? --- the idea was to make it as immune to SAC as possible when it came down to winning or losing a game. Ghhhk is just a better call here. Also lets me play the exterior 2/1 site which has good game text (free movement to the docking bay) and Blizzard 4, which is just a damn good card.

Matchups:

vs Throne Room: one of the hardest matchups. He can come down against your guys with three or four guys and your hit-and-overflow tactic doesn't really work all too well. You may try deploying the 1/1 site and stacking space pulling for Ability^3, which seems to work well in theory but I haven't had enough experience in testing to validate this. You also should NEVER set up fast deal against this matchup unless you really want to get smacked in the face, and hard. A smarter play would be to deploy two guys to different sites, play Occupation, then stack one of the sites and move the other guy to join your big baddies. That way, since Throne Room is weak in space to begin with, you can effectively drain for 1 1 and 1 and do one damage with Occupation, which will whittle him down and maybe be enough to win. Cross your fingers that you don't get this matchup -- it worked for me. :)

vs Combat Racing: should be an easy win. Their one effect can't possibly hurt you (usually For Luck, Scrambled or Goo Nee Tay). By the time they have two destinies stacked on their podracer, you are doing at least ten damage to them (drains of 1, 3, 3, and 3) and possibly 11 if you have the sector, 13 if you have Occupation or the fourth site out (altogether possible considering the amount of force you activate) or 17 with both (18 if you have the sector too). That's ridiculously incomprehensible, but awesome too. Since combat is slow and usually sticks to its own sites with crap like Yoda you should feel relatively safe that he can't throw enough stuff at you to get past your two Ghhhks for overflow.

vs high-destiny Combat: this is a closer game since your deck deploys way more and LS is so efficient. Set up Deal as soon as you can since LS likely only plays a limited number of guys. Be careful with where you deploy your Jedi. You have a lot of 1's but also several 6s and 7s and can flip his objective and hold it for a turn or two if you can track, thus limiting his drains where he has a Jedi. You should hold space unchallenged or virtually unchallenged all game. Dengar/Zuckuss at the system means he won't bust your immunity or forfeit (Dengar and ship forfeit for 10 total) even with Han, Chewie, Falcon making an appearance. Occupation is the kicker here, along with Ability^3, which is huge.

vs Local Uprising: do not deploy the system. Do not deploy the system. Never deploy the system. Menace Fades is what the LS player relies on in this matchup and you cannot give him a system to run to hold it. Drop all your ships to the system, at least two by turn 2 if you can, then set up at will. Occupation is meaningless in this matchup anyway so so is Bespin. If he's playing matching speeders, which everyone is now with this deck, you are safe inside and likely safe outside once Deal is set up. This should be an easy game but practice if you expect to see LU (v) at a local tournament.

vs LS Senate: If Squadron Assignments is started, be wary. Be very wary! If it's not, then your space package will be more than enough. If it is, this game may be painful. With all his power adding and destiny modifying your head will be in a spin and your ships will all be in the lost pile unless you're careful. If your hand is stacked with ships/pilots, take over space as soon as you can. That's the best thing you can do. You could try to bait the opponent into dropping his entire force into your one lone Reegesk, but if that doesn't happen, your second-best bet is to pull Bad Feeling early and load up with Occupation like in the Throne Room matchup. This is another tough matchup if he is heavy in space.

vs Dagobah, MBO, WHAP or any other rogue or degenerate deck that doesn't have a lotof guys to challenge you: you clober him with your speed and immunity to stupid LS tricks.

Thanks for reading and good luck! Like every deck it has its weaknesses but played well, this deck should have enough weapons for you to tackle virtually any light side deck in the current meta.

Jonny Chu
